paragraphs: 8bit-GPT uses an obsolete Macintosh interface to make familiar chatbot interactions feel unfamiliar. The project responds to concerns that dependence on convenient conversational assistants can weaken information retention and encourage superficial emotional attachment. Its purpose is to make people reflect on their relationship with these systems and on language that presents them as humanlike.

The work simulates a language model within a legacy Macintosh operating system and deliberately prioritizes inefficient interaction. It draws on slow technology and counterfunctionality: design approaches that introduce friction to encourage reflection. Here, the mismatch between a familiar conversational tool and an outdated computing environment becomes part of the experience.

The intended effect is to foreground the chatbot as a tool and make its presentation more noticeable. This is a reflective design intervention whose contribution lies in the interaction it stages. The abstract describes an aim to provoke reconsideration of human–AI relationships; it does not report that the installation reduced dependence or changed users’ emotional attachments.
neurips-2025-8bit-gpt-exploring-human-ai.tldr: 8bit-GPT uses a deliberately inefficient legacy Macintosh interface to provoke reflection on chatbot dependence and humanlike framing.

paragraphs: A(I)nimism explores how AI might change people’s relationships with everyday objects by giving those objects conversational personas. Its starting point is animism, in which humans relate to nonhuman beings and things as persons with spirit. The project brings that orientation into an interactive installation concerned with empathy, wonder, and responsibility.

The installation places a system inside a physical portal and combines GPT-4 Vision, voice input, and agents with memory. Together, these components create object personas that can evolve through interaction. Light, sound, and touch organize encounters into a ritual-like sequence of making a request, conversing, and experiencing a transformation.

The paper situates this experience within anthropology, speculative design, and spiritual approaches to human–computer interaction. Its argument is that the difficulty of understanding AI’s internal operation can invite animistic interpretations. The installation makes that possibility tangible, asking how apparently responsive objects might reshape ideas of agency and care. Empathy and reflection are design intentions here, rather than reported measurements of participants’ responses.
neurips-2025-a-i-nimism-re-enchanting-th.tldr: A(I)nimism gives everyday objects evolving AI personas within a ritual-like installation exploring empathy, agency, and animistic relationships.

paragraphs: This project extends Avendish so artists can run machine learning models inside real-time media art environments through a common interface. It addresses a practical obstacle: incorporating AI into an artwork can involve managing Python dependencies and connecting software systems that were not designed together. The proposed bridge uses an open-source C++ library.

An abstraction layer built on onnxruntime lets artists compile models into portable C++ libraries for creative coding environments. The library supports 15 production-ready models covering computer vision, style transfer, emotion recognition, and language capabilities. The selection reflects two years of observing requested AI capabilities in projects at a major media arts research center.

The authors demonstrate integration with ossia score and discuss how this packaging supports real-time use and lowers technical barriers. They also connect portability with preserving artworks whose operation depends on AI models. The contribution is a deployment interface and model collection shaped by artistic practice, bringing existing AI capabilities closer to the software environments in which artists build and maintain their work.
neurips-2025-an-inference-zoo-for-real-t.tldr: Avendish packages 15 AI models behind a portable C++ interface to simplify their use in real-time media artworks.

paragraphs: Artificial Spectator asks what happens when AI becomes an audience for the media it helps produce. The project starts from a mismatch between growing volumes of synthetic content and limited human attention. It proposes artificial viewers as a speculative intervention through which to examine the meaning of attention and aesthetic engagement.

The implementation uses multimodal language models to simulate viewing experiences. These viewers generate emotional responses and internal dialogue, while facial expressions are rendered in real time. Feedback loops connect the simulated emotional state with dialogue generation, allowing each viewing entity’s responses to develop as it processes AI-generated content.

The resulting system gives a concrete form to questions about automated consumption. Producing facial reactions and commentary makes machine attention visible, but the paper treats whether such attention constitutes meaningful engagement as an open question. Its contribution is therefore both an implementation and a critical design exercise: it explores the implications of a media ecosystem in which machines can occupy the roles of creator and spectator.
neurips-2025-artificial-spectator-develo.tldr: Artificial Spectator simulates AI viewers’ emotions, thoughts, and facial reactions to question what automated media engagement could mean.

paragraphs: ArtPeer addresses a gap between producing an attractive image and following the artistic ideas behind a reference. A prompt inspired by an artist, artwork, or movement can lose its intended symbolism or conceptual logic through ambiguity, model biases, or hallucinations. The framework makes reflection part of the image generation process.

It constructs a simulated artist persona from knowledge of biography, style, and iconography. This persona serves as a specialized critic that questions a generation agent through a Socratic dialogue. By identifying departures from the intended inspiration, the agents repeatedly revise the prompt, aiming to bring both visual style and conceptual meaning into alignment.

The authors report qualitative and quantitative evaluations in challenging settings, finding more meaningful and contextually relevant alignment than existing state-of-the-art methods. The significance is that artistic guidance enters through an ongoing critique process, rather than being confined to the initial instruction. The simulated persona supplies a structured source of feedback about the artistic context the generated image is meant to express.
neurips-2025-artpeer-artistic-alignment-.tldr: ArtPeer uses simulated artist critics to iteratively refine image prompts, improving reported stylistic and conceptual alignment with artistic inspiration.

paragraphs: BioArtlas maps relationships among 81 bioart works across thirteen curated dimensions. Bioart combines artistic, scientific, technological, ethical, and political concerns, making a single organizing category inadequate. The project represents these dimensions in a way that preserves their different meanings while allowing works to be compared across them.

A codebook groups related concepts and addresses cultural terms that can carry multiple meanings. The author evaluates up to 800 combinations of representations, spaces, and clustering algorithms. Among these, agglomerative clustering with 15 groups in a four-dimensional UMAP representation performs best, with a reported silhouette score of 0.664 ± 0.008 and trustworthiness and continuity scores of 0.805 and 0.812.

The resulting groups reveal shared methods within artists’ practices, divisions associated with techniques, changes over time, and conceptual connections across periods. These patterns provide several complementary ways to navigate the collection. BioArtlas separates the computational choices used for analysis from public presentation, offering an interactive website for exploration and a publicly available dataset.
neurips-2025-bioartlas-computational-clu.tldr: BioArtlas clusters 81 bioart works across thirteen dimensions, revealing relationships involving artists, techniques, historical change, and cross-period concepts.

paragraphs: CraftGraffiti creates graffiti-style images while trying to keep the depicted person recognizable. This is difficult because strong abstraction and contrast can alter facial features enough to obscure identity. The system takes an input image and a prompt describing the desired style and pose, making facial preservation a central design objective.

Its pipeline first applies graffiti styling with a pretrained diffusion transformer adapted using LoRA. It then reinforces identity through self-attention layers augmented with explicit identity embeddings. Pose changes use CLIP-guided prompt extension without requiring keypoints. This ordering lets the system establish the requested visual treatment before enforcing consistency with the subject’s face.

The authors provide formal justification and empirical evidence that applying style before identity preservation reduces attribute drift compared with reversing those stages. They report competitive facial consistency and state-of-the-art aesthetic and human preference scores. Qualitative analysis and a deployment at the Cruïlla Festival further illustrate its creative use. Together, the results support the proposed sequence as a way to combine substantial stylistic transformation with recognizable facial identity.
neurips-2025-craftgraffiti-exploring-hum.tldr: CraftGraffiti applies graffiti style before reinforcing facial identity, reducing reported attribute drift while supporting prompt-based pose customization.

paragraphs: Echoes of Humanity investigates how listeners distinguish AI-generated songs from human-made music. Participants hear pairs of songs in a blind, Turing-like test and identify which song was generated by AI. The study focuses on the conditions shaping that judgment as well as the musical cues people describe using.

The researchers use a randomized controlled crossover design that controls for similarity within each song pair. This design supports a causal interpretation of the effect of pairwise similarity. They also use AI songs drawn from real-world use of the commercial service Suno, with a dataset whose generation was not controlled by the study’s authors.

The central finding is that listeners become more reliable at identifying the AI song when the paired songs are similar. This makes the construction of comparison pairs consequential for interpreting listening tests. A mixed-methods analysis of participants’ written feedback finds that vocal and technical cues feature prominently in their decisions. These observations can inform both education about recognizing AI music and efforts to improve music generation models.
neurips-2025-echoes-of-humanity-explorin.tldr: A controlled listening study finds that similar song pairs causally improve listeners’ ability to distinguish AI music from human-made music.

paragraphs: EmoNest is a framework for interactive stories that adapt to a user’s emotional state and personal background. It treats storytelling as an experience shaped jointly by the user and the AI. Personalization therefore concerns both what the story contains and how the narrative develops during the interaction.

The framework combines language and vision models with user profiling and real-time narrative adaptation. These components bring information about the person into the generation process, allowing stories to reflect emotional and biographical context. The user’s involvement is part of the creative process, with the system supporting co-creation of immersive narratives intended to feel engaging and emotionally resonant.

The paper presents EmoNest as a demonstration of the potential for personalized artistic experiences and discusses its relevance to emotionally intelligent AI. Its contribution connects generative storytelling with responsiveness to the individual participant. The stated outcome is a framework and demonstration of that potential; the abstract’s emphasis is on enabling emotionally adaptive experiences rather than establishing a quantified improvement in emotional understanding.
neurips-2025-emonest-crafting-emotionall.tldr: EmoNest combines language and vision models with user profiling to co-create stories that adapt to emotional state and personal background.

paragraphs: This paper examines AI creativity through chess compositions, where an appealing puzzle can combine originality, challenge, and an unexpected solution. The underlying system is designed to generate puzzles with aesthetic appeal, novelty, counter-intuitive play, and unique solutions. The paper concentrates on expert interpretation of selected outputs, with technical methodology discussed in a separate paper.

The authors give a curated booklet of generated puzzles to three experts: Amatzia Avni, Jonathan Levitt, and Matthew Sadler. Each has written about chess aesthetics or computers in chess. They select favorite puzzles and explain their appeal, considering creativity, difficulty, and aesthetic design rather than providing only an overall judgment.

The paper brings those selections together with expert analysis of what makes the positions surprising and beautiful. This approach makes the assessment concrete: readers can connect a claim about creativity to particular features of a puzzle and its solution. The contribution is an expert-guided exploration of creative qualities in curated AI compositions, with the experts’ explanations central to understanding their judgments.
neurips-2025-evaluating-in-silico-creati.tldr: Three chess experts select and analyze AI-generated puzzles to explore the qualities that make them creative, challenging, and aesthetically appealing.

paragraphs: Somatic Machine Translation explores how a remembered bodily movement can become material for reflection through a robotic artwork. Such memories can be private and difficult to express. The project begins with a person physically re-enacting a remembered movement, drawing on the role of re-enactment in body-centered therapeutic practices.

An inertial measurement unit captures the movement. A large language model interprets it into natural-language descriptions, which then lead to new movement sequences performed by a robotic sculpture. Language forms the intermediate step between the person’s action and the robot’s response, giving the transformation an explicitly interpretive character.

The authors argue that differences introduced through interpretation and a nonhuman performing body can open new perspectives on bodily memory. The artwork is situated among therapeutic dreamwork, creative AI, and embodied interaction, without presenting a claim of demonstrated therapeutic effectiveness. Its contributions are the movement generation pipeline and a conceptual framework for physical transformation, treating the robot’s changed rendition as a possible resource for reflection.
neurips-2025-from-movement-memories-to-r.tldr: Somatic Machine Translation turns re-enacted movement memories into language and robotic motion to explore new perspectives on bodily experience.

paragraphs: Knolling Bot studies tidying as a problem of understanding human aesthetic preferences. A domestic robot needs a sense of what an orderly arrangement looks like as well as the ability to move objects. The paper focuses on knolling: organizing scattered items into neat layouts that use space efficiently.

The method treats arrangement as a sequence of predictions, drawing inspiration from natural language processing. A transformer-based model forecasts each object’s placement. This formulation addresses household settings in which object collections vary and people may disagree about the most pleasing or appropriate arrangement.

The authors report that their method learns a generalizable concept of tidiness, produces varied solutions for different object sets, and incorporates human preferences to personalize the results. The significance is a way to represent an aesthetic judgment within the robot’s arrangement process. Its stated scope is simple tidying through knolling, presented as a step toward domestic robots that can participate in shaping living spaces according to human tastes.
neurips-2025-knolling-bot-teaching-robot.tldr: Knolling Bot predicts object placements sequentially to create tidy, space-efficient arrangements that accommodate different objects and human preferences.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how to identify the training examples that contributed most to a particular piece of AI-generated music. That task, called training data attribution, is relevant to recognizing the artists whose work informs a model’s output. The authors explore attribution through unlearning, using access to the model’s internals.

They apply the approach to a text-to-music diffusion model trained on a large dataset. Their evaluation examines feasibility and behavior in this setting, using a grid search across hyperparameter configurations and quantitative checks of consistency. They also compare the resulting attribution patterns with approaches that do not use counterfactual analysis.

The findings suggest that unlearning-based attribution can be adapted effectively to music generation at this scale. This supports a technical route toward connecting generated outputs with influential training material. The broader motivation is fairer acknowledgment and greater accountability in AI music, while the reported contribution concerns the feasibility and consistency of an attribution method rather than an established system for assigning artistic credit or resolving copyright questions.
neurips-2025-large-scale-training-data-a.tldr: The paper finds evidence that unlearning can support large-scale attribution of generated music to influential training examples.

paragraphs: Live Music Models introduces music generators that produce a continuous stream while accepting synchronized user control. The central idea is to make interaction part of the music’s ongoing creation. This places the human participant inside the generation process and makes the models relevant to live musical performance.

The authors release Magenta RealTime with open weights. Users can steer its acoustic style through text or audio prompts. On automatic measures of music quality, it outperforms other open-weights music generation models despite having fewer parameters. The paper also presents its live generation capability as a first of its kind.

A second release, Lyria RealTime, provides API access to the authors’ most powerful model, with broader prompt coverage and additional controls. Together, the models illustrate an approach to AI-assisted music making organized around continuous generation and human direction. The reported quality comparison concerns automatic metrics for Magenta RealTime; the broader creative contribution is the ability to shape a musical stream as it unfolds.
neurips-2025-live-music-models-a1ec66994.tldr: Magenta RealTime and Lyria RealTime generate continuous music streams that users can steer during live creation.

paragraphs: MCP2OSC connects natural-language requests with OpenSoundControl, a protocol used to control multimedia systems. The work addresses a practical tension: prompts can be easy to express but imprecise, while knobs and sliders offer fine control at the cost of complexity. It aims to combine conversational access with detailed parameter control.

The authors introduce a Model Context Protocol server and prompt design criteria, demonstrating them through 15 practical question-and-answer examples. With Claude connected to the server, the system generates OSC messages, interprets and searches them, creates visualizations, checks and debugs messages, and manages OSC address patterns. The paper also supplies generalized prompt templates and best practices.

The study reports that this combination handles those OSC tasks effectively. Its contribution places the language model at the protocol level, where it can directly work with human-readable control messages. This provides an interface for creative technical work and suggests the possibility of a broader language-based multimedia control mechanism, while that universal role remains a potential application.
neurips-2025-mcp2osc-parametric-control-.tldr: MCP2OSC connects Claude to OpenSoundControl so natural-language prompts can generate, inspect, debug, and manage multimedia control messages.

paragraphs: This paper develops storytelling systems in which narratives emerge from interactions among language-model-driven characters. Two artworks and video games, Conflicts and The Game of Whispers, demonstrate the approach. The characters combine persistent memory, behavioral models, and coordination to produce coherent stories through simulated social dynamics.

The architecture organizes memory into working memory, episodic buffers, and consolidated narrative storage. A conversation graph tracks central topics, engagement, and unresolved questions. A hybrid orchestrator combines that graph with language-model reasoning to guide the agents’ autonomy. Embodied agents also use a streaming multimodal loop connecting perception with action, supporting awareness of space and responsiveness to their environment.

Experiments reveal strategic deception, coalition formation, misinformation spreading, and awareness of the developing narrative. These behaviors illustrate how the architecture can sustain social interactions with consequences for the story. The contribution is a collection of architectural patterns for stable emergent narrative systems, connecting memory and conversational coordination with characters that act within a shared environment.
neurips-2025-orchestrating-emergent-stor.tldr: A coordinated architecture of embodied language-model agents produces emergent stories featuring behaviors such as deception, coalition formation, and misinformation.

paragraphs: Panel-by-Panel Souls addresses the difficulty of communicating nuanced manga facial expressions through words. A text description can leave the intended emotion ambiguous, making it hard for image generation systems to express a particular narrative moment. The paper introduces an interactive workflow that lets artists guide expressions through performance.

The first stage prepares the face by combining automatic landmark detection with a manual framing tool. This gives the artist a role in establishing the facial region used by the system. The second stage uses LivePortrait to map expressions from video, bringing performed facial movements into the process as a source of fine-grained control.

Case study analysis suggests that the combined workflow can streamline creation and translate narrative intent into visual expressions effectively. The contribution is the integration of tools and artist interaction, rather than a newly developed generative model. Its significance is a more direct connection between the expression an artist performs and the expression assigned to a character, reducing reliance on verbal descriptions alone.
neurips-2025-panel-by-panel-souls-a-perf.tldr: An interactive manga workflow combines face preparation with video-driven expression mapping to help artists convey nuanced narrative intent.

paragraphs: Plan Before You Write introduces a framework that gives language models an explicit process for planning and carrying out writing tasks. It breaks writing into multiple subtasks and includes reflection steps that repeatedly refine the plan. The approach makes planning something the system can revise and execute systematically.

The framework has two uses: it can coordinate multiple model calls to produce writing, or it can generate examples for supervised fine-tuning. To assess writing quality, the authors develop automated raters trained on questions derived from guidelines and filtered by humans. They also gather human judgments to evaluate the resulting writing.

The authors report that outputs produced with the framework are better than outputs from models without a planning component. Human assessments support that finding, with 79.4% of participants ranking the framework’s outputs as more interesting. This result connects the structured planning process to a reader-facing quality of the writing, while the two application routes make the framework relevant both during generation and during training.
neurips-2025-plan-before-you-write-impro.tldr: Iteratively refined writing plans improve reported LLM writing quality, with 79.4% of human participants finding the framework’s outputs more interesting.

paragraphs: This drawing system interprets both how a sketch is constructed and what its content means. The paper calls these formal and contextual intent. Formal intent includes structure, composition, and style; contextual intent covers semantic and thematic meaning. Combining them gives the generation process access to more of what participants express through drawing.

The system analyzes line trajectories, proportions, and spatial arrangement alongside semantic cues extracted with vision–language models. A multi-stage pipeline uses both signals, combining structural control that preserves contours with image synthesis sensitive to style and content. The sketch therefore provides geometric guidance as well as information about the intended subject.

A touchscreen interface and distributed inference architecture support a low-latency, two-stage transformation process. Multiple participants can work together on shared canvases, enabling synchronous visual co-creation across levels of artistic expertise. The contribution connects interpretation of the drawing with the practical interaction system, allowing users’ marks and shared participation to guide generated imagery in real time.
neurips-2025-real-time-intuitive-ai-draw.tldr: A real-time collaborative drawing system combines sketch geometry and semantic meaning to guide AI transformations on shared canvases.

paragraphs: Studies for is a generative sound installation developed with sound artist Evala. It explores an archive that preserves an artist’s style while continuing to produce new material. The artwork uses SpecMaskGIT, a lightweight sound generation model, to generate and play eight-channel audio in real time during a three-month exhibition.

The model is trained on more than 200 hours of Evala’s previous sound artworks. That material provides the basis for reflecting the artist’s identity while generating previously unheard sounds. The archive concept therefore combines continuity with the artist’s existing practice and the inclusion of unexpected outputs that extend beyond the past works.

The study emphasizes artist feedback, training datasets drawn from the artist’s work, and room for novelty as key requirements for this form of co-creation. It proposes a framework for incorporating sound generation into artistic practice. The installation also motivates a speculative possibility: generative archives could continue expanding an artist’s sound world beyond their physical existence, while retaining a connection to their artistic style.
neurips-2025-studies-for-a-human-ai-co-c.tldr: Studies for uses Evala’s past sound artworks to generate live eight-channel audio, exploring an archive that preserves style while creating new sounds.

paragraphs: This paper examines how musicians can retain a sense of ownership when composing with AI. It studies a music variation tool in a four-week ecological evaluation, placing the tool within a composition setting. The focus is the relationship between the musician’s skill, the tool’s role, and ownership of the creative process and resulting music.

The tool depends on musicians to provide strong initial musical material and to develop promising moments into complete ideas. The study finds that these demands on human ability promote ownership. Musical judgment remains important at both ends of the interaction: shaping what the tool receives and deciding how its contributions become a composition.

Qualitative interviews reinforce the importance of personal ownership and reveal tensions between technological capability and artistic identity. The findings suggest that dependence on the musician’s craft can be a valuable design feature. In this setting, AI-supported variation contributes to creativity while leaving meaningful compositional work with the musician, helping preserve a sense that both the process and the artifact are their own.
neurips-2025-supporting-creative-ownersh.tldr: A four-week study finds that an AI music variation tool’s reliance on musicians’ skills promotes ownership of the process and composition.

paragraphs: The Stochastic Parrot explores an AI interface that shares a person’s physical environment and acts with its own character. The authors call this an AI cohabitant: an agent that can initiate activity without a user command and develop a personality, narrative, and rhythm of interaction.

They embody the concept in a robotic parrot. Its continuous physical presence creates opportunities for the AI to observe, learn, and participate in everyday life. The design frames interaction around living alongside a characterful entity, with a degree of autonomy, rather than around opening an application or explicitly requesting each response.

The authors report observing new interaction patterns and more nuanced relationships between the parrot and its human counterpart. They argue that physical embodiment and the framing of a living presence invite spontaneous, expressive, and emotionally textured engagement. The project’s contribution is this interface concept and its concrete exploration, making the AI’s ongoing presence and character central to how a relationship with it develops.
neurips-2025-the-stochastic-parrot-a-phy.tldr: A robotic parrot explores AI cohabitation, where physical presence, personality, and autonomous behavior shape ongoing human–AI relationships.

paragraphs: TinyTim is a family of language models designed to supply divergent language within larger systems. The authors argue that training centered on accepted solutions encourages convergence and restricts creative reframing. They pursue a different generative style by fine-tuning on the unusually expansive language of James Joyce’s Finnegans Wake.

The study examines an unsupervised fine-tuned model, TinyTim-V1, and an instruction-tuned version, TinyTim-V2. Quantitative analysis finds strong lexical invention. The authors report that V1’s Yule’s K score, used in their analysis of lexical richness, exceeds convergent baselines by more than twentyfold. V2 retains a statistically distinct profile and resists factual convergence despite instruction tuning.

That persistence comes with a stated tradeoff: V2 sacrifices benchmark performance to preserve its generative style. The paper proposes combining specialized divergent models with convergent systems to support conceptual reframing. Its quantitative evidence concerns lexical behavior and the stability of that behavior across the family; the authors connect these properties to a broader argument about engineering components for creative breakthroughs.
neurips-2025-tinytim-a-family-of-languag.tldr: TinyTim models fine-tuned on Finnegans Wake exhibit persistent lexical invention, with instruction tuning preserving that style at a cost to benchmark performance.

paragraphs: EarthCanvas approaches satellite image reconstruction as a tool for environmental storytelling. Clouds, missing observations, and sensor failures can fragment imagery, making it harder for communities to use. The framework is designed for educators, journalists, and advocates who want to create accessible accounts of environmental change.

It combines three components. Terrain-aware conditioning supports geographic authenticity, natural-language prompts let non-experts guide climate narratives, and a visual harmony module helps synthetic and real imagery fit together coherently. These components connect the reconstruction process with the needs of people communicating environmental issues, emphasizing both scientific fidelity and cultural relevance.

The authors report strong reconstruction performance and a 40% improvement in comprehension and engagement in user studies. These findings connect image restoration with how people understand and engage with the resulting narratives. The contribution is a framework for human–AI participation in environmental communication, treating coherent imagery and accessible creative control as parts of the same storytelling task.
neurips-2025-visualizing-our-changing-ea.tldr: EarthCanvas combines satellite reconstruction with language-guided storytelling, reporting strong reconstruction and a 40% improvement in user comprehension and engagement.

paragraphs: Writing in Symbiosis examines how creative writing changes alongside the growing presence of language models. It analyzes a large longitudinal corpus spanning periods before and after their emergence. The paper questions whether these changes are adequately described as stylistic homogenization, looking for different patterns of adaptation across authors.

The observed patterns suggest two simultaneous developments: greater thematic attention to AI and structured differences in stylistic change. Some authors become more similar to AI style, others become less similar, and another group maintains a stable style while engaging with AI-related themes. The authors organize these patterns into a Creative Archetype Map.

This map distinguishes what writers discuss from how they write. A shared interest in AI-related subjects can coexist with multiple stylistic trajectories, complicating a single account of convergence. The findings are presented as suggestive patterns of human–AI coevolution. They contribute to discussions of creative agency, diversity, and AI detection by showing why thematic overlap and stylistic similarity need to be considered separately.
neurips-2025-writing-in-symbiosis-mappin.tldr: Longitudinal writing analysis suggests convergence on AI-related themes alongside distinct patterns of stylistic convergence, divergence, and stability.
